title: Museums of fine art and their public
titleCn: Museums of fine art and their public
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: Museums of fine art and their public

The fact that people go to the Louvre museum in Paris to see the original painting Mona Lisa when they can see a reproduction anywhere leads us to question some assumptions about the role of museums of fine art in today's world

One of the most famous works of art in the world is Leonardo Da Vinci's Mona Lisa. Nearly everyone who goes to see the original will already be familiar with it from reproductions, but they accept that fine art is more rewardingly viewed in its original form.

However, if Mona Lisa was a famous novel, few people would bother to go to a museum to read the writer's actual manuscript rather than a printed reproduction. This might be explained by the fact that the novel has evolved precisely because of technological developments that made it possible to print out huge numbers of texts, whereas oil painting have always been produced as unique objects. In addition, it could be argued that the practice of interpreting or 'reading' each medium follows different conventions. With novels, the reader attends mainly to the meaning of words rather than the way they are printed on the page, whereas the 'reader' of a painting must attend just as closely to the material form of marks and shapes in the picture as to any ideas they may signify.

Yet it has always been possible to make very accurate facsimiles of pretty well any fine art work. The seven surviving versions of Mona Lisa bear witness to the fact that in the 16th century, artists seemed perfectly content to assign the reproduction of their creations to their workshop apprentices as regular 'bread and butter' work. And today the task of reproducing pictures is incomparably more simple and reliable, with reprographic techniques that allow the production of high-quality prints made exactly to the original scale, with faithful colour values, and even with duplication of the surface relief of the painting.
But despite an implicit recognition that the spread of good reproductions can be culturally valuable, museums continue to promote the special status of original work.
Unfortunately, this seems to place severe limitations on the kind of experience offered to visitors.

One limitation is related to the way the museum presents its exhibits. As repositories of unique historical objects, art museums are often called 'treasure houses'. We are reminded of this even before we view a collection by the presence of security guards, attendants, ropes and display cases to keep us away from the exhibits. In many cases, the architectural style of the building further reinforces that notion. In addition, a major collection like that of London's National Gallery is housed in numerous rooms, each with dozens of works, any one of which is likely to be worth more than all the average visitor possesses. In a society that judges the personal status of the individual so much by their material worth, it is therefore difficult not to be impressed by one's own relative 'worthlessness' in such an environment.

Furthermore, consideration of the 'value' of the original work in its treasure house setting impresses upon the viewer that, since these works were originally produced, they have been assigned a huge monetary value by some person or institution more powerful than themselves. Evidently, nothing the viewer thinks about the work is going to alter that value, and so today's viewer is deterred from trying to extend that spontaneous, immediate, self-reliant kind of reading which would originally have met the work.

The visitor may then be struck by the strangeness of seeing such diverse paintings, drawings and sculptures brought together in an environment for which they were not originally created. This 'displacement effect' is further heightened by the sheer volume of exhibits. In the case of a major collection, there are probably more works on display that we could realistically view in weeks or even months.

This is particularly distressing because time seems to be a vital factor in the appreciation of all art forms. A fundamental difference between paintings and other art forms is that there is no prescribed time over which a painting is viewed. By contrast, the audience encounters an opera or a play over a specific time, which is the duration of the performance. Similarly, novels and poems are read in a prescribed temporal sequence, whereas a picture has no clear place at which to start viewing, or at which to finish. Thus art works themselves encourage us to view them superficially, without appreciating the richness of detail and labour that is involved.

Consequently, the dominant critical approach becomes that of the art historian, a specialized academic approach devoted to 'discovering the meaning' of art within the cultural context of its time. This is in perfect harmony with the museum`s function, since the approach is dedicated to seeking out and conserving 'authentic', 'original' readings of the exhibits. Again, this seems to put paid to that spontaneous, participatory criticism which can be found in abundance in criticism of classic works of literature, but is absent from most art history.

The displays of art museums serve as a warning of what critical practices can emerge when spontaneous criticism is suppressed. The museum public, like any other audience, experience art more rewardingly when given the confidence to express their views. If appropriate works of fine art could be rendered permanently accessible to the public by means of high-fidelity reproductions, as literature and music already are, the public may feel somewhat less in awe of them. Unfortunately, that may be too much to ask from those who seek to maintain and control the art establishment.

Choose the correct answer and move it into the gap.

定位词：availability of novels, so long

第二段第二句：题目问的是人们到博物馆并不需要读到小说最初的手稿，这是由于小说长久依赖依靠什么。这一信息在文章第二段中有涉及，可以看到句中说到the novel has evolved precisely because of technological developments that made it possible to print out huge numbers of texts,也就是说这是由于技术发展使得人们可以print out huge numbers of text,因此在选项中寻找这一表达的同义替换，可以看到B项的mass production与其含义一致，因此本题答案为B。

定位词：novels, the most important thing

groups.contextHtml:
The value attached to original works of art

People go to art museums because they accept the value of seeing an original work of art. But they do not go to museums to read original manuscripts of novels, perhaps because the availability of novels has depended on [27] ______ for so long, and also because with novels, the [28] ______ are the most important thing.

However, in historical times artists such as Leonardo were happy to instruct [29] ______ to produce copies of their work and these days new methods of reproduction allow excellent replication of surface relief features as well as colour and [30] ______ .

It is regrettable that museums still promote the superiority of original works of art, since this may not be in the interests of the [31] ______ .

questions.prompt: The writer mentions London`s National Gallery to illustrate

options.text: the undesirable cost to a nation of maintaining a huge collection of art.
the conflict that may arise in society between financial and artistic values.
the negative effect a museum can have on visitors` opinions of themselves.
the need to put individual well-being above large-scale artistic schemes.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者提到伦敦国家美术馆是为了说明_______。

定位词：London's National Gallery

A一个国家不值得花费如此多成本来维护如巨量的艺术品。

B社会上可能出现的财政和艺术价值之间的冲突。

C博物馆可能存在的关于参观者对自身态度上的负面作用。

D相比大规模的艺术品，更需要关注个体的感受。

本题首先可以通过题目中的London's National Gallery在原文中确定考查区域，之后在这一信息所在的第六段中，分析London's National Gallery出现的目的。通过上下文的分析，可以看到由于艺术品展出的形式以及其价值，参观者会对自身产生负面的感觉,也就是本段最后一句中的"worthlessness"这与C项中的表达一致。因此本题答案为C。

questions.prompt: The writer says that today, viewers may be unwilling to criticize a work because

options.text: they lack the knowledge needed to support an opinion.
they fear it may have financial implications.
they have no real concept of the work's value.
they feel their personal reaction is of no significance.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者说，如今参观者或许不希望评论一件作品是因为

定位词：unwilling to criticize

A他们缺少支持观点所需要的知识。

B他们担心作品有经济意义。

C他们对作品的价值没有真正的概念。

D他们感到自己的个人反应并不重要。

关于参观者不愿意评论作品的原因出现在文章第七段，其中说到Evidently, nothing the viewer thinks about the work is going to alter that value, and so today's viewer is deterred from trying to extend that spontaneous, immediate, self-reliant kind of reading which would originally have met the work, 可见，由于作品的价值很高，人们认为自已的想法和评论不会产生任何影响，因此unwilling to criticise,这与D项的表述一致。因此本题答案为D。

questions.prompt: According to the writer, the 'displacement effect' on the visitor is caused by

options.text: the variety of works on display and the way they are arranged.
the impossibility of viewing particular works of art over a long period.
the similar nature of the paintings and the lack of great works.
the inappropriate nature of the individual works selected for exhibition.

questions.explanation:
译文：根据作者的观点，参观者的“位移效应”是由_____引起的。

定位词：'displacement effect'

A展出艺术品的种类以及它们被放置的方式。

B不可能长时间观赏特定的艺术作品。

C图画近似的性质以及缺少伟大作品。

D作品不适合被选择进行展出。

题目中的'displacement effect'出现在文章第八段第二句话，本句开头使用This 'displacement effect' is further heightened by这一结构，因此需要在上下文中分析相关的表达，可以看到，这种情况的产生是由于大量的作品在并非为它们创造的环境中同时被展示，选项中A的表述与之一致。因此本题答案为A。

questions.prompt: The writer says that unlike other forms of art, a painting does not

options.text: involve direct contact with an audience.
require a specific location for a performance.
need the involvement of other professionals.
have a specific beginning or end.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者说不像其他艺术形式，一幅绘画作品不会。

定位词：unlike other forms of art

A包含与观众的直接接触。

B要求特定的展出地点。

C需要包含其专业性。

D有特定的开始和结束。

关于美术作品与其他艺术形式的差别出现在文章第九段，即A fundamental difference between paintings and other art forms is that there is no prescribed time over which a painting is viewed, 之后又进行了具体的解释，这与D项的表述一致，因此本题答案为D。

groups.instruction:
Questions 36-40

Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

Choose YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer,

choose NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer,

or choose NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

questions.prompt: Art history should focus on discovering the meaning of art using a range of media.
questions.explanation:
参考译文：艺术史应当关注使用各种媒介发现艺术品的意义。

定位词：art history

本题关注的是art history通过a range of media来发现艺术品的意义，在文中的表述中，只在第十段说到艺术史学家使用的方法是一种a specialised academic approach devoted to "discovering the meaning' of art within the cultural context of its time,而并没有出现| art history借助a range of media, 因此本题答案为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: The approach of art historians conflicts with that of art museums.
questions.explanation:
定位词：approach, art historians, art museums

本题问的是艺术史学家的方法和艺术博物馆的方法是否矛盾。艺术史学家的方法在文章第十段有明确的表述: Consequently, the dominant critical approach becomes that of the art historian, a specialised academic approach devoted to 'discovering the meaning' of art within the cultural context of is time, 后文接着说: This is in perfect harmony with the museum's function,其中in harmony with意思是“与.......协调、一致”，所以二者是一致的，并非相互矛盾，因此本题答案为NO。

questions.prompt: People should be encouraged to give their opinions openly on works of art.
questions.explanation:
参考译文：应当鼓励人们对艺术作品开放性地给出自己的观点。

定位词：give their opinions

从本文最后几段表达的观点来看，由于art historian和art museum, 人们的spontaneous, participatory criticism受到了限制，而作者认为，人们应当更开放地表达自己的观点，其中第十一段写到The museum public like any other audience, experience art more rewardingly when given the confidence to express their views.这与题目的表达一致，因此本题答案为YES。

questions.prompt: Reproductions of fine art should only be sold to the public if they are of high quality.
questions.explanation:
参考译文：如果具备很高的品质，艺术品的复制品应当仅仅售卖给人们。

定位词：reproduction of fine art

本题问到是否高品质的复制品只应该售卖给人们，通过对第38题出题位置之后部分的阅读可知，文中并没有表达是否售卖的问题，也就是说作者并没有就这个问题表达明确的观点。 因此本题答案为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: In the future, those with power are likely to encourage more people to enjoy art.
questions.explanation:
参考译文：将来，那些有权势的人很有可能去鼓励更多的人欣赏艺术。

定位词：those with power

本题重点问的是those with power,因此需要找到这类人对于艺术的态度，看他们是否鼓励更多的人欣赏艺术。根据文章最后一段的表述，可以看到实际上那些希望维持和控制艺术的人并没有意愿让更多的人欣赏艺术: If appropriate works of fine art could be rendered permanently accessible to the public by means of high-fidelity reproductions, as literature and music already are, the public may feel somewhat less in awe of them. Unfortunately, that may be too much to ask from those who seek to maintain and control the art establishment.此处Unfortunately起到了转折的作用，之后的表达比较明确地说明了这类人的态度。因此本题答案为NO。

articleHtml:
Museums of fine art and their public

The fact that people go to the Louvre museum in Paris to see the original painting Mona Lisa when they can see a reproduction anywhere leads us to question some assumptions about the role of museums of fine art in today's world

One of the most famous works of art in the world is Leonardo Da Vinci's Mona Lisa. Nearly everyone who goes to see the original will already be familiar with it from reproductions, but they accept that fine art is more rewardingly viewed in its original form.

However, if Mona Lisa was a famous novel, few people would bother to go to a museum to read the writer's actual manuscript rather than a printed reproduction. This might be explained by the fact that the novel has evolved precisely because of technological developments that made it possible to print out huge numbers of texts, whereas oil painting have always been produced as unique objects. In addition, it could be argued that the practice of interpreting or 'reading' each medium follows different conventions. With novels, the reader attends mainly to the meaning of words rather than the way they are printed on the page, whereas the 'reader' of a painting must attend just as closely to the material form of marks and shapes in the picture as to any ideas they may signify.

Yet it has always been possible to make very accurate facsimiles of pretty well any fine art work. The seven surviving versions of Mona Lisa bear witness to the fact that in the 16th century, artists seemed perfectly content to assign the reproduction of their creations to their workshop apprentices as regular 'bread and butter' work. And today the task of reproducing pictures is incomparably more simple and reliable, with reprographic techniques that allow the production of high-quality prints made exactly to the original scale, with faithful colour values, and even with duplication of the surface relief of the painting.

But despite an implicit recognition that the spread of good reproductions can be culturally valuable, museums continue to promote the special status of original work.

Unfortunately, this seems to place severe limitations on the kind of experience offered to visitors.

One limitation is related to the way the museum presents its exhibits. As repositories of unique historical objects, art museums are often called 'treasure houses'. We are reminded of this even before we view a collection by the presence of security guards, attendants, ropes and display cases to keep us away from the exhibits. In many cases, the architectural style of the building further reinforces that notion. In addition, a major collection like that of London's National Gallery is housed in numerous rooms, each with dozens of works, any one of which is likely to be worth more than all the average visitor possesses. In a society that judges the personal status of the individual so much by their material worth, it is therefore difficult not to be impressed by one's own relative 'worthlessness' in such an environment.

Furthermore, consideration of the 'value' of the original work in its treasure house setting impresses upon the viewer that, since these works were originally produced, they have been assigned a huge monetary value by some person or institution more powerful than themselves. Evidently, nothing the viewer thinks about the work is going to alter that value, and so today's viewer is deterred from trying to extend that spontaneous, immediate, self-reliant kind of reading which would originally have met the work.

The visitor may then be struck by the strangeness of seeing such diverse paintings, drawings and sculptures brought together in an environment for which they were not originally created. This 'displacement effect' is further heightened by the sheer volume of exhibits. In the case of a major collection, there are probably more works on display that we could realistically view in weeks or even months.

This is particularly distressing because time seems to be a vital factor in the appreciation of all art forms. A fundamental difference between paintings and other art forms is that there is no prescribed time over which a painting is viewed. By contrast, the audience encounters an opera or a play over a specific time, which is the duration of the performance. Similarly, novels and poems are read in a prescribed temporal sequence, whereas a picture has no clear place at which to start viewing, or at which to finish. Thus art works themselves encourage us to view them superficially, without appreciating the richness of detail and labour that is involved.

Consequently, the dominant critical approach becomes that of the art historian, a specialized academic approach devoted to 'discovering the meaning' of art within the cultural context of its time. This is in perfect harmony with the museum`s function, since the approach is dedicated to seeking out and conserving 'authentic', 'original' readings of the exhibits. Again, this seems to put paid to that spontaneous, participatory criticism which can be found in abundance in criticism of classic works of literature, but is absent from most art history.

The displays of art museums serve as a warning of what critical practices can emerge when spontaneous criticism is suppressed. The museum public, like any other audience, experience art more rewardingly when given the confidence to express their views. If appropriate works of fine art could be rendered permanently accessible to the public by means of high-fidelity reproductions, as literature and music already are, the public may feel somewhat less in awe of them. Unfortunately, that may be too much to ask from those who seek to maintain and control the art establishment.
